text: Christianity is the world's largest religion, with approximately 2.4 billion adherents spanning every continent on Earth.
Islam is the world's second-largest religion, with around 1.9 billion Muslims, and it is also the fastest-growing major religion globally.
Hinduism is one of the world's oldest living religions, with roots dating back over 4,000 years to the Indus Valley Civilization, and has approximately 1.2 billion followers today.
Buddhism was founded by Siddhartha Gautama (the Buddha) in the 5th to 4th century BCE in what is now Nepal and northeastern India.
Judaism is one of the oldest monotheistic religions, originating over 3,500 years ago, and forms the foundation from which both Christianity and Islam developed.
Sikhism was founded in the Punjab region of South Asia in the 15th century CE by Guru Nanak Dev Ji and today has approximately 25–30 million followers worldwide.
Jainism, one of India's oldest religions, teaches non-violence (ahimsa) as its supreme ethical principle and has around 4–5 million adherents, predominantly in India.
Zoroastrianism, one of the world's oldest monotheistic religions, was founded by the prophet Zoroaster (Zarathustra) in ancient Iran and profoundly influenced the Abrahamic faiths.

Taoism (Daoism) is a Chinese philosophical and religious tradition emphasizing harmony with the Tao (the Way), with its foundational text, the Tao Te Ching, attributed to the sage Laozi around the 4th century BCE.
Shinto is the indigenous spirituality of Japan, centered on the worship of kami (spirits), and uniquely has no official founder, no single sacred scripture, and no fixed creed.
The Bahá'í Faith, founded in 19th-century Persia, teaches the unity of all major religions and the oneness of humanity, with its world administrative center in Haifa, Israel.
The Bible is the best-selling book of all time, with an estimated 5 billion copies distributed since 1815, according to the Guinness World Records.
The Quran, Islam's holy scripture, is believed by Muslims to be the verbatim word of God as revealed to the Prophet Muhammad over approximately 23 years via the Angel Gabriel.
The Rigveda, part of the Hindu sacred Vedas, is one of the oldest known religious texts in the world, composed between 1500 and 1200 BCE in Vedic Sanskrit.
The Tipitaka (Pali Canon) is the earliest complete collection of Buddhist scriptures preserved in the Pali language; it contains the teachings of Theravada Buddhism across three 'baskets' of text.
The Torah comprises the five books of Moses (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) and forms the bedrock of Jewish law and religious scripture.

The Guru Granth Sahib, the eternal living Guru of the Sikhs, contains compositions by six Sikh Gurus as well as verses from Hindu bhakti saints and Sufi Muslim poets, reflecting its inclusive theology.
Mecca, in present-day Saudi Arabia, is Islam's holiest city; non-Muslims are prohibited from entering its central area, and over 2 million pilgrims converge there annually for the Hajj.
Jerusalem is sacred to three Abrahamic faiths simultaneously: it houses the Western Wall (Judaism), the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (Christianity), and the Dome of the Rock (Islam).
The Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca is one of Islam's Five Pillars and must be performed at least once in a lifetime by every able-bodied Muslim who can afford to do so.
The Kumbh Mela is the world's largest religious gathering; the 2019 Prayagraj Kumbh Mela attracted an estimated 200 million visitors over 49 days, a fact recognized by the Guinness World Records.
Vatican City, headquarters of the Roman Catholic Church and residence of the Pope, is the world's smallest internationally recognized sovereign state at just 44 hectares within Rome.

Christmas, celebrating the birth of Jesus Christ on December 25, is the most widely observed religious festival in the world, celebrated by approximately 2 billion people across Christian and secular traditions.
Diwali, the Hindu Festival of Lights, is celebrated over five days and symbolizes the spiritual victory of light over darkness, knowledge over ignorance, and good over evil.
Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic lunar calendar, during which Muslims fast from dawn to sunset; the month commemorates the first revelation of the Quran to Muhammad.
Passover (Pesach) commemorates the liberation of the Israelites from Egyptian slavery as described in the Book of Exodus and is observed for seven or eight days with a ritual Seder meal.
Vesak (Buddha Day) is the most sacred Buddhist holiday, commemorating the birth, enlightenment, and death of the Buddha; it is observed by millions across Asia and recognized by the United Nations.
Vaisakhi (Baisakhi) marks the founding of the Khalsa Panth (the Sikh brotherhood) by Guru Gobind Singh Ji on April 13, 1699, and is one of Sikhism's most important annual celebrations.
The Five Pillars of Islam are Shahada (declaration of faith), Salah (five daily prayers), Zakat (charitable giving of 2.5% of savings), Sawm (Ramadan fasting), and Hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca).

The Four Noble Truths of Buddhism identify suffering (dukkha) as inherent in existence, trace its origin to craving, declare it can be ended, and prescribe the Eightfold Path as the means to achieve that end.
The concept of karma, originating in Hinduism and central to Buddhism and Jainism, holds that a person's actions directly determine their fate in future existences within the cycle of rebirth.
The Dead Sea Scrolls, discovered between 1947 and 1956 near the Dead Sea, include the oldest known manuscripts of the Hebrew Bible, dating from roughly the 3rd century BCE to the 1st century CE.
The First Council of Nicaea in 325 CE, convened by Emperor Constantine I, established the Nicene Creed, defining core Christian doctrine including the Trinity and the nature of Jesus Christ.
The Protestant Reformation began in 1517 when Martin Luther published his Ninety-Five Theses challenging the Catholic Church's sale of indulgences, splitting Western Christianity permanently.
The 14th Dalai Lama, Tenzin Gyatso, is the spiritual leader of Tibetan Buddhism and was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989 for his nonviolent campaign for Tibetan freedom.
The Golden Temple (Harmandir Sahib) in Amritsar, India, is Sikhism's holiest shrine and serves a free communal meal (langar) to more than 100,000 visitors daily regardless of religion or caste.

The Bodhi Tree in Bodh Gaya, India, is a sacred fig tree (Ficus religiosa) under which the Buddha is said to have attained enlightenment; the current tree is considered a direct descendant of the original.

The Camino de Santiago (Way of St. James) is a network of pilgrimage routes leading to the Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in Spain, where the remains of the Apostle James are traditionally believed to rest.

Confucianism, based on the teachings of Confucius (551–479 BCE), emphasizes family loyalty, social harmony, and ritual propriety and has profoundly shaped Chinese, Korean, Japanese, and Vietnamese cultures for over two millennia.
The Mahabharata, one of Hinduism's two great Sanskrit epics, is the world's longest poem at approximately 1.8 million words—more than ten times the combined length of Homer's Iliad and Odyssey.
The Bhagavad Gita, a 700-verse Hindu scripture embedded within the Mahabharata, presents a dialogue between Prince Arjuna and the god Krishna on duty, righteousness, and spiritual paths.
The Talmud is a central text of Rabbinic Judaism comprising the Mishnah and Gemara; compiled over several centuries, it covers Jewish law, ethics, philosophy, history, and legend.

Marduk was the chief deity of ancient Babylonian religion; his supremacy is celebrated in the Enuma Elish, one of the earliest known creation narratives in human history, predating the biblical Genesis.

The Sufi tradition within Islam emphasizes the inner, mystical dimension of the faith; the 13th-century Sufi poet Rumi, known for the Masnavi, remains one of the best-selling poets in the United States.
The Amarnath Cave in Jammu & Kashmir, India, is one of Hinduism's holiest shrines, housing a naturally formed ice Shivalingam that waxes and wanes with the lunar cycle each year.
The Eastern Orthodox Church separated from the Roman Catholic Church in 1054 CE in the Great Schism, primarily over disputes regarding papal authority and the theological filioque clause.
Zoroastrian sacred fire temples called Atash Bahrams house flames that have been kept continuously burning for over 1,500 years; several such temples still operate in Yazd, Iran.
Many Eastern Orthodox Christians celebrate Christmas on January 7 because they follow the Julian calendar, which runs 13 days behind the Gregorian calendar used by Western Christianity.
Yom Kippur, the Jewish Day of Atonement, is considered the holiest day of the Jewish year and is observed with a 25-hour fast and intensive synagogue prayer services.
Lent is a 40-day period of fasting, prayer, and penance in Christianity leading up to Easter, commemorating the 40 days Jesus spent fasting and praying in the desert.
Zakat, one of Islam's Five Pillars, requires Muslims with sufficient wealth to donate 2.5% of their accumulated savings annually to those in need, making charitable giving a religious obligation.
The Western Wall (Wailing Wall) in Jerusalem is the holiest site where Jews are permitted to pray; it is the last surviving outer wall of the Second Temple complex, destroyed by Rome in 70 CE.
Nirvana in Buddhism refers to the transcendent state free from suffering, desire, and individual ego, representing liberation from the cycle of death and rebirth (samsara).

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS), founded by Joseph Smith in 1830 in upstate New York, has grown to over 17 million members worldwide and is headquartered in Salt Lake City, Utah.
