The Council of Trent (1545–1563), convened in response to the Protestant Reformation, reaffirmed Catholic doctrines and standardized the Latin Tridentine Mass, which remained the universal Roman Catholic liturgy until the Second Vatican Council (1962–1965) introduced the vernacular Mass, the most significant liturgical change in 400 years.

Swami Vivekananda's famous address at the World's Parliament of Religions in Chicago in 1893, beginning with 'Sisters and Brothers of America,' received a two-minute standing ovation and was credited with introducing Hinduism, yoga, and Vedanta philosophy to a mass Western audience for the first time.

The Hindu concept of Maya — often translated as 'illusion' — does not mean the world doesn't exist but rather that we mistake the material world for ultimate reality; for Advaita Vedanta philosopher Adi Shankaracharya (8th century CE), only Brahman (the universal consciousness) is ultimately real, and the appearance of a world of separate objects is Maya.

The practice of circumcision as a religious rite is found in Judaism (since Abraham's covenant, approximately 2000 BCE), Islam (as a Sunnah practice), and numerous African indigenous traditions; the Jewish brit milah ceremony is performed on the eighth day after birth, a timing that modern medicine notes coincides with naturally elevated Vitamin K clotting factors in newborns.

The Nicene Creed, the common statement of faith used by most Christian denominations, was originally formulated at the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE) and expanded at the First Council of Constantinople (381 CE); the addition of 'and the Son' (filioque) to describe the Holy Spirit's procession by the Western Church became a central issue in the Great Schism of 1054.

Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, undertook four major journeys (udasis) covering thousands of miles on foot across South Asia, the Middle East, and Central Asia — including visits to Mecca and Baghdad — engaging in spiritual discussions with Hindu, Muslim, and Buddhist leaders; these travels shaped Sikhism's profoundly pluralistic theology.

The concept of papal infallibility — that the Pope speaks without error when formally defining doctrines of faith and morals ex cathedra — was formally defined only at the First Vatican Council in 1870; it has been invoked only once since then, in 1950, when Pope Pius XII defined the dogma of the Assumption of Mary.

The Islamic Golden Age (8th–13th centuries CE) saw Muslim scholars preserve and extend classical Greek philosophy, mathematics, and medicine; Muslim philosophers such as Ibn Rushd (Averroes) wrote commentaries on Aristotle so influential that they sparked the recovery of Aristotelian thought in medieval European universities through Latin translation.

The Hindu pilgrimage site of Varanasi (Kashi/Benares) on the Ganges River is considered the holiest city in Hinduism; dying and being cremated there is believed to guarantee moksha (liberation from the cycle of rebirth), drawing pilgrims from across India who come to die, and the city's cremation ghats have been burning continuously for over 3,000 years.

The Bahá'í concept of 'Progressive Revelation' holds that God has sent a series of divine messengers (including Abraham, Moses, Krishna, Zoroaster, Buddha, Jesus, Muhammad, and Bahá'u'lláh) each bringing teachings appropriate to the capacity of their age; each messenger's dispensation is seen as a chapter in a continuing divine plan for humanity.

The Sikh institution of Langar (community kitchen) serves free meals to all visitors regardless of caste, religion, or social status; this practice, established by Guru Nanak, was intended to undermine the caste hierarchy by having all people sit together on the floor and eat the same simple vegetarian food.

The Masnavi (or Mathnawi), composed by the 13th-century Sufi poet Jalal al-Din Rumi, is a 25,000-verse Persian poem exploring spiritual themes through parables, anecdotes, and commentary on the Quran; it has been called the 'Persian Quran' by admirers and remains one of the greatest works of mystical literature ever written.

The ancient Mesopotamian religion included the Epic of Gilgamesh, containing a flood narrative — the story of Utnapishtim — that predates and closely parallels the Genesis account of Noah's Ark; the Gilgamesh flood tablet was discovered in 1872 by George Smith at the British Museum, causing a sensation in the Victorian world.

The Shakers, formally the United Society of Believers in Christ's Second Appearing, were a celibate Christian communal sect founded by Ann Lee in 18th-century England; their elaborate ritualistic dances (giving them the name 'Shakers') produced remarkably simple, elegant furniture now prized as American folk art, but celibacy made them dependent on conversion and adoption, leading to their near extinction.

The Hindu ashram system divides an ideal human life into four stages (ashramas): Brahmacharya (student, celibate study), Grihastha (householder, family life), Vanaprastha (forest-dweller, gradual retirement), and Sannyasa (renunciant, total withdrawal from worldly life); this framework remains influential in Indian culture though strictly followed by relatively few.

The Theravada Buddhist practice of monks going on alms rounds (pindapata) every morning — collecting food offerings from laypeople in silence — creates a ritual exchange where monks provide spiritual merit to donors and in turn receive physical sustenance; this symbiotic relationship between the monastic and lay community has sustained Theravada Buddhism for 2,500 years.

The Armenian Genocide of 1915–1916, in which the Ottoman Empire killed an estimated 600,000 to 1.5 million Armenian Christians, is regarded by the Armenian Apostolic Church and the Armenian diaspora as a religious as well as ethnic persecution; Pope Francis described it in 2015 as 'the first genocide of the 20th century,' drawing sharp protests from Turkey.

The Islamic prohibition on depictions of the Prophet Muhammad, derived from hadith traditions against image-making, is not explicitly stated in the Quran; many historical Muslim societies did produce images of the Prophet, particularly in Persian miniature painting, though strict Sunni orthodoxy has consistently prohibited such representations.

The Dongba religion of China's Naxi people uses the world's only living pictographic writing system — Dongba script — which has over 1,400 pictographs; Dongba shamans (dongba) memorize sacred texts and conduct elaborate rituals for healing, funerals, and appeasing nature spirits in this endangered tradition now recognized by UNESCO.

The Jansenist heresy in 17th-century Catholicism, developed from Cornelius Jansen's interpretation of Augustine, held that human nature is totally corrupted and that God grants irresistible saving grace only to the predestined elect; condemned by Pope Innocent X in 1653, Jansenism persisted in France and produced Blaise Pascal as one of its famous adherents.

The Hindu concept of Moksha (liberation) is understood differently by different philosophical schools: Advaita Vedanta sees it as merging with Brahman (the universal consciousness), Dvaita Vedanta views it as eternal loving union with but distinct from God, and Vishishtadvaita sees the liberated soul as part of God but maintaining individual identity.

The Church of the Flying Spaghetti Monster (Pastafarianism), founded by Bobby Henderson in 2005 as a satirical response to the teaching of intelligent design in Kansas public schools, has been legally recognized as a religion in the Netherlands and New Zealand; its adherents wear colanders on their heads in official ID photos as religious headgear.

The Sikh tradition of Kirtan (devotional music) is considered an active form of meditation and worship; the Harimandir Sahib (Golden Temple) has kirtan performed continuously 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, by ragis (professional musicians) who sing hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib in classical Indian ragas.

The Mandukya Upanishad, the shortest of the major Upanishads at just 12 verses, analyzes the syllable OM as encompassing all of reality through four states of consciousness: waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the transcendent fourth state (turiya); the 8th-century philosopher Gaudapada's commentary on it became foundational for Advaita Vedanta.

The historical Exodus of Israelites from Egypt, central to Jewish, Christian, and Islamic traditions, is not corroborated by Egyptian historical records; most archaeologists and historians believe the biblical narrative is a composite of historical memories, theological interpretation, and legendary elaboration rather than a literal account of a single mass migration.

The concept of Tikkun Olam (Hebrew: 'repair of the world') originated in Kabbalistic contexts but was popularized in 20th-century American Judaism as a mandate for social justice activism; it has become one of the most commonly cited Jewish values in progressive politics, though traditionalists note it has been largely stripped of its original mystical meaning.

The Confucian concept of Ren (humaneness or benevolence) is expressed in the negative Golden Rule: 'Do not impose on others what you yourself do not want' (Analects 15:24); Confucius placed Ren at the core of all moral cultivation, describing it as the highest virtue from which all others flow.

The medieval Islamic city of Timbuktu in Mali was a major center of Islamic scholarship from the 13th to 17th centuries, containing over 100,000 manuscripts on theology, law, mathematics, and astronomy; the Ahmed Baba Institute now holds approximately 30,000 of these manuscripts, many still awaiting scholarly examination.

The Zoroastrian conception of time is divided into three cosmic eras: Bundahishn (good creation), the assault of Ahriman (the evil principle), and the ultimate Frashokereti (renovation of the world) in which evil is annihilated and the dead are resurrected into a perfect, immortal existence — a linear eschatology that likely influenced Jewish, Christian, and Islamic apocalypticism.

The Sunni–Shia split in Islam traces to the dispute over succession after Muhammad's death in 632 CE; Sunnis accepted Abu Bakr as the first caliph (successor) while Shia Muslims (Shi'at Ali, partisans of Ali) believed leadership should pass through Ali ibn Abi Talib, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and his descendants.

The Cave of Machpelah (Tomb of the Patriarchs) in Hebron is sacred to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam as the burial site of Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebecca, and Jacob and Leah; it is one of the world's most contested holy sites, divided between a mosque and a synagogue after an Israeli-Palestinian agreement following the 1994 Cave of Machpelah massacre.

In Native American Lakota spirituality, the sweat lodge (inipi) ceremony involves pouring water over heated stones inside a dome-shaped lodge to create steam, representing purification, prayer, and rebirth from the womb of Mother Earth; the ceremony is considered one of the seven sacred rites given to the people by the spirit White Buffalo Calf Woman.

The Hindu Char Dham pilgrimage circuit encompasses four sacred dhams (abodes) at the four geographic corners of India: Badrinath (north), Dwarka (west), Puri (east), and Rameswaram (south); completing the circuit is believed to wash away all sins and aid in achieving moksha.

The Digambara sect of Jainism, one of the two major Jain traditions, holds that monastic renunciation is so complete that monks must give up all possessions — including clothing; male Digambara monks live entirely naked as a symbol of total non-attachment, a practice rejected by the Shvetambara ('white-clad') Jain sect.

Eid al-Adha (Feast of the Sacrifice), one of Islam's two major festivals, commemorates Abraham's willingness to sacrifice his son (Ishmael in Islamic tradition, Isaac in Jewish and Christian traditions) and God's provision of a ram as substitute; Muslims who can afford to do so slaughter a livestock animal and distribute its meat to family, neighbors, and the poor.

The Vedanta Society, founded in New York in 1894 by Swami Vivekananda, was the first Hindu organization to establish permanent centers in the West; it introduced practices like meditation and yoga as spiritual disciplines accessible to non-Indians, transforming them from esoteric Indian traditions into global wellness practices.

The Trappist monastic order (Order of Cistercians of the Strict Observance) maintains a near-vow of silence and practices manual labor; Trappist monasteries are famous for their high-quality commercial products — especially beer — with Trappist beers from Belgian abbeys like Westvleteren and Rochefort ranking among the world's most sought-after craft beverages.

The Quran is divided into 114 chapters (surahs) arranged roughly from longest to shortest rather than in chronological order of revelation; the longest surah, Al-Baqarah (The Cow), contains 286 verses, while the shortest, Al-Kawthar (Abundance), has only 3 — yet the 3-verse surah is considered among the most profound in Islamic mysticism.

The Gnostic Gospel of Thomas, discovered at Nag Hammadi in Egypt in 1945, contains 114 sayings attributed to Jesus with no narrative structure; many sayings parallel the canonical Gospels but others are found nowhere else, and scholars debate whether it preserves authentic early Jesus traditions independent of the canonical Gospels.

The Theravada Buddhist tradition of forest monks (Araññavasi) emphasizes solitary meditation in forests, caves, and charnel grounds over monastic scholarship; the Thai Forest Tradition, revitalized by Ajahn Mun Bhuridatta (1870–1949), has produced some of the 20th century's most revered meditation teachers including Ajahn Chah and Ajahn Thanissaro.

The Hindu concept of the four Purusharthas (life's aims) holds that human flourishing encompasses Dharma (righteousness/duty), Artha (wealth/prosperity), Kama (pleasure/desire), and Moksha (liberation); this framework, unique in world religions, explicitly validates the pursuit of wealth and pleasure as legitimate life goals alongside spiritual liberation.

The Cathedral of Chartres in France, built in the High Gothic style (1194–1220 CE), features 176 stained glass windows containing 4,000 individual figures telling biblical and hagiographic stories; it was one of the first buildings to use flying buttresses extensively, allowing the walls to be filled with glass and light as a theological statement about divine illumination.

The Jain Mahavira, the 24th and final Tirthankara (ford-maker/spiritual conqueror) of the current cosmic cycle, was a contemporary of the Buddha (c. 599–527 BCE); like the Buddha, he was a prince who renounced his royal life, but unlike the Buddha, Mahavira practiced extreme physical austerities including standing in the sun for hours and remaining motionless for long periods.

The Sufi tariqa (spiritual path or order) system channels discipleship through a silsila (chain) of transmission stretching back through generations of masters to Muhammad; major orders include the Qadiriyya (founded by Abd al-Qadir al-Jilani, d. 1166), Naqshbandiyya, Mevlevi, and Chishti, each with distinct practices of dhikr (divine remembrance).

The Hindu Kumbh Mela cycle occurs at four sacred river confluences in India (Prayagraj, Haridwar, Nashik, and Ujjain) based on the positions of Jupiter, the Sun, and Moon; the Purna (full) Kumbh at Prayagraj occurs every 12 years, while the Maha (great) Kumbh comes every 144 years — the most recent was in 2013.

Transcendental Meditation (TM), developed by Maharishi Mahesh Yogi in India in the 1950s and brought to global attention when the Beatles visited Maharishi's ashram in Rishikesh in 1968, uses personally assigned mantras for 20-minute twice-daily meditation sessions; over 600 peer-reviewed studies have examined its claimed physiological and psychological benefits.

The Hindu goddess Kali, the fierce form of Durga, is depicted with black skin, a garland of severed heads, and a severed head in one hand; despite her terrifying appearance, her devotees worship her as the most compassionate goddess — her destruction is directed at the ego and the illusion of separateness, not at the devotee.

The Psalms in the Hebrew Bible/Christian Old Testament are a collection of 150 religious poems and songs attributed primarily to King David; they were used as the liturgical hymnbook of the Second Temple and remain central to Jewish and Christian prayer, with the early Christian monk John Cassian recommending monks memorize all 150 psalms.

The Crusades (1095–1291), launched by Pope Urban II's call at the Council of Clermont, were a series of religiously sanctioned military campaigns aimed at capturing Jerusalem from Muslim rule; their legacy includes the transfer of Greek scientific and philosophical texts to Europe, but also massacres of Jews, Muslims, and Eastern Christians.

The Islamic concept of Sharia (divine law) encompasses far more than criminal punishments; the vast majority of Sharia law deals with personal religious practice, family relations, contracts, and ethics — the dramatic hudud punishments (amputation for theft, stoning for adultery) represent a small fraction of the overall legal system and require extremely high standards of evidence.

The Yoruba religion of West Africa features an elaborate pantheon of 401+ orishas (divine spirits); enslaved Africans brought Yoruba religion to the Americas where it syncretized with Catholicism to produce Candomblé in Brazil, Santería (Lucumí) in Cuba, and Trinidadian Shango — all of which remain vibrant living traditions.

Thomas Aquinas's Five Ways (Quinque Viae) in the Summa Theologica present five arguments for God's existence: the argument from motion (unmoved mover), from causation (first cause), from contingency (necessary being), from gradation (perfect being), and from teleology (intelligent designer) — these arguments remain central to Catholic natural theology.

The Masoretes, a group of Jewish scribal scholars who worked mainly in Tiberias between the 7th and 10th centuries CE, standardized the Hebrew text of the Bible by adding vowel markers and cantillation marks to the consonantal text; the Masoretic Text became the authoritative basis for both Jewish and most Protestant Old Testament translations.

The Sikh concept of Waheguru (Wondrous Teacher/God) is considered beyond gender, form, and human comprehension; the Mool Mantar, the opening verse of the Guru Granth Sahib, describes God as 'the One Being, whose Name is Truth, the Creative Force, Without Fear, Without Hate, Timeless, Self-Existent, Realized through the Guru's Grace.'

The spread of Buddhism along the Silk Road trade routes connected India, Central Asia, China, Korea, and Japan; this transmission was facilitated not just by missionaries but by merchant communities who built Buddhist stupas and cave complexes along trade routes, including the Dunhuang Caves in China's Gansu Province, which preserve tens of thousands of Buddhist manuscripts and artworks.

The concept of Samsara — the continuous cycle of death, rebirth, and redeath — is central to Hinduism, Buddhism, and Jainism; while all three traditions agree that Samsara is driven by karma and that liberation from it is the ultimate spiritual goal, they differ fundamentally about what constitutes liberation and who or what is reborn.

The Inca religion centered on the sun god Inti, whose son the Sapa Inca (emperor) was believed to be on Earth; the vast Temple of the Sun (Coricancha) in Cusco had its walls covered in gold sheets representing the sun, and at its center was a solid gold statue of Inti; the Spanish conquistadors melted nearly all the gold on arrival.

The Daoist concept of Wu Wei (non-action or effortless action) does not mean doing nothing but rather acting in perfect harmony with the natural flow of the Tao; it is illustrated in the Tao Te Ching with the image of water, which overcomes rock not by force but by persistent, yielding flow.

The Templo Mayor (Great Temple) of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan (present-day Mexico City) was discovered beneath the streets only in 1978 during utility work; excavations have revealed seven superimposed temples (each new emperor built a new shell around the existing structure) and thousands of ritual offerings including jaguar remains, obsidian knives, and coral.

The Great Mosque of Cordoba (Mezquita) in Spain, built between the 8th and 10th centuries CE, is considered one of the finest examples of Umayyad architecture; after the Reconquista in 1236, a Catholic cathedral was built inside it, creating one of the world's most striking architectural examples of religious layering and cultural succession.

The Charvaka school of ancient Indian philosophy (c. 600 BCE) was one of the world's earliest systematic atheist and materialist philosophies, rejecting all religious authority, the afterlife, karma, and the soul; it taught that only perception is a valid source of knowledge and that the purpose of life is pleasure — a radical position within Indian philosophical tradition.

The Ethiopian Falasha Beta Israel (House of Israel) Jews practiced Judaism for centuries in isolation from global Jewry; unaware of the Talmud, they followed only the Torah and Apocrypha and observed a form of Temple-era Judaism with priests, sacrifices, and purification rituals; Israeli airlifts (Operations Moses and Solomon) brought most of them to Israel in 1984–85 and 1991.

Comparative religion as an academic discipline was largely founded by Friedrich Max Müller (1823–1900), who edited the 50-volume Sacred Books of the East series, translating Hindu, Buddhist, Zoroastrian, and other scriptures into English; he coined the phrase 'He who knows one religion knows none' to argue that understanding requires comparative study.

The Hindu Tirupati Balaji Temple (Venkateswara Temple) in Andhra Pradesh is the richest religious institution in the world, with an estimated net worth of $30+ billion; it receives about 50,000–100,000 pilgrims daily and collects hundreds of millions of dollars annually in donations — including an estimated $35 million worth of hair offerings from devotees per year.

The Christian doctrine of Atonement — how Jesus's death reconciles humanity with God — has multiple competing theories: the ransom theory (Christ's death paid a ransom to Satan), Anselm's satisfaction theory (honor debt to God), the moral influence theory (inspiring transformation), and penal substitution (Christ bore humanity's punishment in its place).

Ancestor veneration — honoring and communicating with deceased family members through rituals, offerings, and shrines — is practiced across Chinese (as Qingming and Ghost Festival), Japanese (as Obon), Korean (as Chuseok), and many African and indigenous traditions; anthropologists consider it one of the world's most widespread religious practices, found in nearly every major cultural tradition.

The Baha'i House of Worship (Mashriqu'l-Adhkár), called the Lotus Temple in New Delhi and completed in 1986, is shaped like a lotus flower and receives over 10,000 visitors daily — more than any other building in India; it is open to all people regardless of religion and has no clergy, sermons, or rituals, offering only silent prayer and scripture reading.

The Zen Buddhist koan — a paradoxical question or statement used as a meditation object, such as 'What is the sound of one hand clapping?' — was systematized by the Song dynasty Chinese master Dahui Zonggao (1089–1163); koans are designed to defeat conceptual thinking and provoke direct insight into the nature of mind.

The Cao Daist Great Divine Temple (Tòa Thánh) in Tây Ninh Province, Vietnam, is a spectacular architectural blend of a Buddhist pagoda, Catholic cathedral, Taoist temple, and Disney castle; inside, portraits of Victor Hugo, Sun Yat-sen, and Nguyen Binh Khiem hang together as saints who revealed Cao Dai teachings through Ouija-board-style séances.

The Tibetan Buddhist practice of creating sand mandalas — intricate geometric representations of enlightened mind produced over days using millions of grains of colored sand — is ritually destroyed upon completion, with the sand swept into a river; this deliberate destruction embodies the Buddhist teaching of impermanence (anicca).

The Jewish Shema Yisrael ('Hear O Israel, the Lord is our God, the Lord is One') from Deuteronomy 6:4 is considered Judaism's central declaration of faith and is recited in morning and evening prayers, on one's deathbed, and written in the mezuzah scrolls affixed to Jewish doorposts; it is the first prayer Jewish children are taught.

The Islamic doctrine of Isra and Mi'raj describes the Prophet Muhammad's miraculous Night Journey from Mecca to Jerusalem (Isra) and his ascension through the seven heavens to the divine throne (Mi'raj); the Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem marks the site from which Muhammad is believed to have ascended, making it the third holiest site in Islam.

The Nestorian Church (Church of the East) spread Christianity as far as China, India, and Central Asia in the 7th–13th centuries, reaching Tang dynasty China by 635 CE as recorded on the Xi'an Stele; it was one of the most extensive missionary movements in pre-modern history, though most of its Central Asian communities were destroyed by Timur's conquests in the 14th century.

The Rastafarian practice of wearing dreadlocks (referred to as 'locs') is rooted in a Nazirite vow from Numbers 6:5 ('No razor shall come upon his head') and in solidarity with Kenyan Mau Mau fighters; reggae musicians like Bob Marley globalized dreadlocks as a symbol of Rastafarian spirituality and Africanidentity.

Christian mysticism — found in the Desert Fathers, Meister Eckhart, Julian of Norwich, John of the Cross, and Teresa of Avila — emphasizes direct personal experience of God beyond doctrine; the 'Dark Night of the Soul' described by John of the Cross as a period of spiritual desolation preceding divine union has been applied by psychologists including William James as a model of transformative religious experience.

The African traditional religion of the Zulu people of South Africa centers on Unkulunkulu, the creator and first man, and communication with amadlozi (ancestral spirits) through a diviner called an isangoma; the isangoma diagnoses spiritual problems through throwing bones and entering trance states, and may be called by the ancestors through illness rather than choosing the role.

The concept of Nirgun Brahman (God without qualities) versus Sagun Brahman (God with qualities) represents a fundamental tension in Hindu theology: the formless, attribute-free Absolute that cannot be described versus the personal God with form who can be worshipped and loved; most Hindu practice mediates between these two in what the philosopher Ramakrishna called a relationship like sugar and a sugar doll.

The Aztec calendar stone (Sunstone), carved around 1479 CE and measuring 3.6 meters in diameter, was rediscovered in Mexico City's main square in 1790; it depicts the four previous suns (cosmic eras) destroyed by catastrophe, and the current fifth sun at the center — a religious-astronomical monument that is now Mexico's most recognized pre-Columbian artifact.

The Protestant concept of sola scriptura (Scripture alone) — that the Bible is the sole infallible authority for Christian faith and practice — was one of the foundational principles of the Reformation; it stood in contrast to the Catholic Church's position that Scripture and Tradition together constitute the sources of divine revelation.

The Hindu epic Ramayana, composed by the sage Valmiki, tells the story of the god-king Rama, his wife Sita, and the demon king Ravana; it exists in over 300 versions across South and Southeast Asia, has profoundly shaped the art, literature, and politics of the region, and remains actively performed in religious contexts from Bali to Thailand to India.

The Quaker William Penn founded Pennsylvania in 1681 as a 'holy experiment' in religious tolerance, guaranteeing freedom of worship to all who believed in God; this made Pennsylvania one of the most religiously diverse colonies in North America and laid groundwork for the First Amendment's religious freedom protections in the US Constitution.

Liberation theology, which emerged in Latin America in the 1960s–70s under theologians like Gustavo Gutiérrez and informed by Vatican II's social teaching, interprets the Gospel through the 'preferential option for the poor' and calls the Church to work for structural social change; it was criticized by Pope John Paul II and the Vatican's Cardinal Ratzinger for incorporating Marxist analysis.

The Sikh martial art of Gatka, practiced since at least the 16th century, uses sticks and swords in choreographed combat routines for spiritual discipline and self-defense; the sixth Sikh Guru, Hargobind Sahib Ji, established the principle of Miri-Piri (temporal and spiritual authority combined) that integrated martial readiness with spiritual practice.

The concept of Puja Darshan in Hinduism — the visual beholding of the divine image in a temple — is considered a two-way exchange: the worshiper sees the deity and the deity sees the worshiper; the god's eyes are opened ceremonially in the installation rite (pratishtha) and the moment of seeing is considered a divine blessing (prasada).

The Spanish Inquisition, established in 1478 by King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella, was a separate institution from the medieval Papal Inquisition; it targeted primarily conversos (Jewish converts to Christianity) suspected of secretly practicing Judaism, and at its height burned at the stake an estimated 3,000–5,000 people over its 350-year existence, though modern historians debate these numbers.

The Quran's description of Paradise (Jannah) includes gardens with rivers of water, milk, honey, and wine (purified, non-intoxicating), beautiful companions, fine clothing, and the greatest joy of all: the vision of God's face (ru'yat Allah); the Islamic tradition extensively debated whether this vision was literal or metaphorical.

Meister Eckhart (c.1260–1328), a Dominican friar and Christian mystic, taught that the soul's innermost ground (Seelenfunklein, the little spark of the soul) is identical with the divine ground; charged with heresy after his death, several of his propositions were condemned by Pope John XXII in 1329 — yet his influence on subsequent mysticism, including Protestant mysticism, was enormous.

The Japanese Buddhist Soka Gakkai (Value Creation Society), founded in 1930 and affiliated with Nichiren Buddhism, is Japan's largest and most politically influential lay Buddhist organization with over 8 million households as members in Japan; its political party, Komeito, is a consistent coalition partner in the Japanese government.

The Sikh turban (dastar or pagri), worn by initiated Khalsa Sikhs, is not merely a cultural garment but a religious commitment representing honor, self-respect, courage, and piety; it covers the uncut hair (kesh), itself one of the Five Ks (panj kakars) that Sikhs wear as physical symbols of faith since Guru Gobind Singh's 1699 institution of the Khalsa.

The Sufi poet Hafiz of Shiraz (c. 1315–1390), whose Divan contains over 500 ghazals (lyric poems) of intense divine love, became one of the most beloved poets in Persian literature; his collection is used as a divination text in Iran (Fal-e Hafez), opened randomly to receive guidance, a tradition similar to the Christian practice of Sortes Biblicae.

The Hindu festival of Navaratri (Nine Nights), dedicated to the goddess Durga, is celebrated twice yearly and culminates in different observances across India: West Bengal celebrates Durga Puja with elaborate clay goddesses; Gujarat performs the Garba and Dandiya Raas dances; and South India honors Saraswati, the goddess of learning.

The concept of the Logos in Christian theology — 'In the beginning was the Word (Logos)' (John 1:1) — drew on the Greek philosophical concept of Logos as the rational principle ordering the cosmos; early Christian theologians like Justin Martyr used this bridge between Greek philosophy and Christian revelation to argue that all rational humans implicitly participate in Christ.

The Jewish holiday of Purim commemorates the story in the Book of Esther in which the Jewish queen of Persia and her cousin Mordecai thwarted Haman's plot to exterminate the Jews; it is unique among Jewish holidays for its carnival atmosphere, requiring Jews to drink until they can no longer distinguish between 'cursed Haman' and 'blessed Mordecai.'

The ancient Indian city of Varanasi is mentioned in the earliest Buddhist texts as Benares, the city where the Buddha gave his first sermon at Deer Park (Sarnath); the sacred geography of the city maps onto a 5-kilometer walking circuit of 108 pilgrimage points called Panchakroshi Yatra, believed to represent the distance between birth and liberation.

New Atheism, a cultural movement that emerged in the mid-2000s with books by Richard Dawkins (The God Delusion, 2006), Christopher Hitchens (God Is Not Great, 2007), and Sam Harris (The End of Faith, 2004), argued that religion is not merely wrong but actively harmful; critics argued these 'New Atheists' caricatured religion and ignored its sociological complexity.

The Sangam literature of ancient Tamil Nadu (c. 300 BCE–300 CE) contains some of the earliest references to distinctly South Indian (Dravidian) religious concepts; it describes a landscape-based spiritual geography (tinai) in which specific regions of land correspond to specific deities, seasons, and emotional states of love — an indigenous Tamil spirituality predating Brahmanical influence.

The Second Vatican Council (1962–1965), convened by Pope John XXIII and continued by Paul VI, was the most significant event in 20th-century Roman Catholicism; it produced documents affirming religious freedom, approving Mass in vernacular languages, declaring that Jews are not collectively guilty for Jesus's death, and promoting ecumenical dialogue with other Christian denominations and religions.

The Rosicrucian Johann Valentin Andreae published the Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreuz in 1616, an allegorical novel describing an alchemical wedding and the hero's initiation into divine mysteries; it spawned the Rosicrucian movement and influenced Freemasonry, the Golden Dawn, and modern Western esotericism.

The Akashic Records, a concept from Theosophy and later popularized in New Age spirituality, refers to a supposed compendium of all universal events, thoughts, words, and emotions encoded in a non-physical plane of existence; the concept draws on the Sanskrit word 'akasha' (sky/ether) and has no basis in mainstream science but remains influential in esoteric traditions.

The Christian denomination of Pentecostalism, born in the Azusa Street Revival in Los Angeles in 1906 under William J. Seymour, teaches that speaking in tongues (glossolalia) is the initial evidence of baptism in the Holy Spirit; it has grown from a small revival meeting into the world's fastest-growing Christian movement with an estimated 500 million to 1 billion adherents.

The Hindu practice of Yoga — systematic mental and physical disciplines aimed at achieving spiritual liberation — dates back to the Indus Valley Civilization's proto-Shiva seated in meditation position (Pashupati seal, c. 2500 BCE); Patanjali's Yoga Sutras (c. 400 CE) systematized it into eight limbs (Ashtanga), of which physical postures (asanas) form only the third.

The Islamic tradition of Ijaz al-Quran (the inimitability of the Quran) holds that the Quran's literary beauty is so unique and perfect that no human could have produced it — itself a miracle proving Muhammad's prophethood; this doctrine has driven the remarkable memorization culture of Islam, with millions of hafiz (memorizers) who have committed all 77,430 words to memory.

The Hasidic dynasty system, in which the title of rebbe passes from father to son, has produced remarkable lineages including the Lubavitch (Chabad), Satmar, and Breslov dynasties; the 18th-century Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, who died without male heirs in 1810, is still revered by his Breslov followers who believe they need no successor — earning them the nickname 'dead Hasidim.'

The Temple Mount in Jerusalem (Har HaBayit in Hebrew, Haram al-Sharif in Arabic) is the world's most contested religious site, sacred to Judaism (site of the First and Second Temples), Islam (third holiest site, location of Al-Aqsa Mosque and Dome of the Rock), and Christianity (where Jesus taught and overturned the money-changers' tables).

The Pauline Epistles — letters attributed to the Apostle Paul in the New Testament — are the earliest Christian texts, predating the Gospels by decades; scholars identify 7 letters as authentically Pauline (c. 48–62 CE) and 6 as deutero-Pauline, and Paul's theological innovations (justification by faith, the universal church, Christ as second Adam) shaped Christianity more than any other writer.

The Japanese concept of kami in Shinto is not equivalent to the Western God; kami can be found in natural phenomena (thunder, mountains, rivers), revered humans (emperors, heroes), ancestral spirits, and abstract forces; the 8th-century text Kojiki (Record of Ancient Matters) lists thousands of kami and describes the mythological origin of Japan and the imperial family.

The Benedictine Abbey of Monte Cassino, founded by St. Benedict of Nursia around 529 CE on a mountain between Rome and Naples, is considered the birthplace of Western monasticism; it was destroyed and rebuilt four times — by Lombards (589), Saracens (883), earthquake (1349), and Allied bombing in 1944 — and each time reconstructed as a symbol of Christian resilience.

The Aztec goddess Tlazolteotl was the deity of filth, sex, and purification — a paradoxical combination reflecting the Aztec view that the same force that generates impurity also cleanses it; her priests heard confessions of sexual sins once in a lifetime, and it was considered wisest to defer this sacrament until old age so that all sins could be absolved at once.

The Sikh scripture's structure includes a section called the Rahao (pause), a refrain that contains the core message of each hymn, around which all other verses revolve; unlike Western musical structures with a beginning-middle-end narrative, this circular structure reflects the Sikh theological concept that all of creation revolves around the divine Name (Naam).

The Oxford Movement (1833–1845), led by John Henry Newman, Edward Pusey, and John Keble at Oxford University, sought to revive Catholic elements within the Church of England; Newman's eventual conversion to Roman Catholicism in 1845 shocked England, and his intellectual journey from Anglican to Catholic was documented in his Apologia Pro Vita Sua, one of the great spiritual autobiographies in English.

The concept of Theodicy — coined by philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in 1710 in his essay Essais de Théodicée — addresses the philosophical problem of why an all-powerful, all-knowing, benevolent God permits evil and suffering; Leibniz's controversial conclusion that this is 'the best of all possible worlds' was famously satirized by Voltaire in Candide (1759).

The Eleusinian Mysteries held at Eleusis near Athens offered initiates a secret experience so transformative that the philosopher Cicero wrote it allowed Athens to give humanity 'not only the means of living joyfully but also of dying with better hope'; modern scholars have proposed that the initiatory drink (kykeon) may have contained ergot fungus with psychedelic alkaloids similar to LSD.

Confucius's Analects (Lunyu), compiled by his disciples after his death in 479 BCE, record his sayings and conversations on ethics, governance, and self-cultivation; Confucius himself claimed no originality, describing himself as a transmitter of ancient wisdom rather than an innovator — yet his synthesis became the dominant intellectual tradition of East Asia for over two millennia.

The Zoroastrian sacred fire maintained at the Iranshah (King of Fires) Atash Behram in Udvada, Gujarat, India, is believed by the Parsi community to have been burning continuously since it was brought by Persian Zoroastrian refugees around 721 CE; it is the holiest of all Parsi sacred fires and the site of annual pilgrimages from across the Parsi diaspora.

The Shia Muslim practice of Tatbir (self-flagellation with chains or blades on Ashura) to mourn Imam Husayn's martyrdom at Karbala is controversial even within Islam; Grand Ayatollah Ali Khamenei issued a fatwa against it in 1994, and it is banned in Iran, though it continues in parts of Iraq, Pakistan, and Lebanon.

The Hindu concept of Avatara (Sanskrit: 'descent') describes the voluntary incarnation of a deity — typically Vishnu — into the material world to restore cosmic order (Dharma) when it is threatened; the Bhagavata Purana lists ten principal avataras (Dashavatara) including Matsya (fish), Kurma (tortoise), Varaha (boar), and eventually Rama, Krishna, and the future Kalki.

The Women's Ordination controversy in the Roman Catholic Church intensified after the Church of England began ordaining women as priests in 1994; Pope John Paul II declared in his 1994 Apostolic Letter Ordinatio Sacerdotalis that the Church has 'no authority whatsoever to confer priestly ordination on women,' which the Vatican subsequently declared an infallible teaching, though many theologians dispute this characterization.

The Jain Palitana temples on Shatrunjaya Hill in Gujarat, India, comprise a complex of 863 temples built over 900 years; the hill is so sacred to Jains that it is illegal to eat, drink, or stay overnight on it, making it one of the few religious sites in the world where the local government enforces religious dietary laws.

The ancient Egyptian concept of Ma'at was so fundamental that pharaohs derived their legitimacy from upholding it; the annual flooding of the Nile, the rising of the sun, and the orderly succession of seasons were all understood as manifestations of Ma'at — the king's primary duty was to maintain this cosmic order through correct ritual and just governance.

The Islamic jurisprudential tradition developed four major Sunni schools of law (madhabs): Hanafi (most widely followed, in Turkey, South Asia, and Central Asia), Maliki (North and West Africa), Shafi'i (East Africa, Southeast Asia), and Hanbali (Arabian Peninsula); despite some differences, all four schools recognize each other as valid interpretations of Islamic law.

Mircea Eliade (1907–1986), the Romanian-American historian of religion, introduced the concept of hierophany — any manifestation of the sacred in the profane world — and argued in The Sacred and the Profane (1957) that religious experience is fundamentally about the distinction between sacred space/time and ordinary space/time; his work remains both influential and contested.

The Buddhist Jataka Tales, a collection of 547 stories about the Buddha's previous lives as animals, humans, and divine beings, served both as moral teaching and as evidence for reincarnation; they profoundly influenced Asian literature and art, with versions traveling from India to Central Asia, Southeast Asia, and even Europe as Aesop's Fables-style moral tales.

The Hindu festival of Ganesh Chaturthi, celebrating the birth of Lord Ganesha, was transformed into a mass public festival by Indian nationalist leader Bal Gangadhar Tilak in 1893 to bring communities together and build solidarity against British colonial rule; it is now one of India's largest festivals, with Mumbai's celebrations drawing millions and involving massive clay Ganesha idols immersed in the sea.

The Lakota concept of the Great Mystery (Wakan Tanka) is often translated as 'Great Spirit,' but more precisely encompasses the totality of the sacred — a unified field of spiritual power that infuses all living things; the Lakota ceremony of the Sun Dance, involving days of fasting and ritual piercing of the skin, is a sacrifice to Wakan Tanka for the good of the people.

The Hindu god Vishnu's vehicle (vahana) is the divine eagle Garuda, while Shiva's is the bull Nandi, Brahma's is the swan (hamsa), and Ganesha's is the mouse (mushika); these animal companions in Hindu iconography function as symbolic attributes that help devotees identify and understand the nature of each deity.

The Salat al-Jumu'ah (Friday noon prayer) is the most important weekly act of communal worship in Islam; the Quran explicitly commands Muslims to leave trading and hasten to the Friday prayer (62:9–10), and the sermon (khutba) delivered by an imam before the prayer has historically served political as well as spiritual functions.

The Augustinian theological tradition, derived from the 4th-5th century Bishop Augustine of Hippo, introduced the doctrine of original sin — inherited guilt and corruption from Adam's fall — and predestination of the elect; these doctrines were developed by Calvinism and Jansenism and became central points of dispute in Protestant-Catholic theological debates.

Angkor Wat in Cambodia, built by the Khmer king Suryavarman II in the early 12th century, is the world's largest religious monument at 402 acres; originally a Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu, it was converted to a Buddhist temple in the late 13th century and remains an active place of Buddhist worship today while serving as a major UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The Book of Job in the Hebrew Bible confronts the problem of innocent suffering without resolving it theologically; God's response to Job from the whirlwind offers no explanation of why the righteous suffer but instead an overwhelming vision of cosmic grandeur — what biblical scholars call a divine 'answer' that ignores Job's question while satisfying his deeper need for encounter with the divine.

The Bodhi Dharma (Bodhidharma), the semi-legendary Indian monk who brought Chan (Zen) Buddhism to China around the 5th–6th centuries CE, is said to have spent nine years meditating facing a wall at the Shaolin Temple, losing the use of his legs; the Shaolin monks subsequently developed Kung Fu exercises to restore their health, making Bodhidharma the legendary founder of both Zen and Chinese martial arts.

The Mormon practice of posthumous baptism — performing proxy baptisms for deceased persons of any religion so they may choose to accept Mormonism in the afterlife — has led to controversy when genealogy records were used to baptize Holocaust victims and other historical figures; the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints maintains extensive genealogical records as part of this doctrine.

The Sufi concept of Dhikr (remembrance of God), performed through repetitive chanting of divine names, is considered the heart of Sufi practice; different orders practice dhikr differently — some silently (khafi), some aloud (jali), some with specific breathing techniques — and the state of absorption in God's name that dhikr produces is considered a form of prayer superior to formal ritual.

The Bon and Buddhist traditions of Tibet both use prayer flags (lung ta, meaning 'wind horse') to spread spiritual blessings and prayers; the five colors represent the five elements (space, air, fire, water, earth) and the five Buddha families, and the printing of mantras on flags is believed to spread their blessings to all beings touched by the wind.

The Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith (CDF), formerly known as the Holy Office or Roman Inquisition (founded 1542), is the Vatican office responsible for safeguarding Catholic doctrine; it issued the controversial 2000 declaration Dominus Iesus, asserting that Catholic Church is the only means of complete salvation, reaffirming that other Christian churches have 'defects.'

The Sufi master Ibn Arabi (1165–1240), known as the 'Greatest Master' (al-Shaykh al-Akbar), developed a comprehensive metaphysical system called Wahdat al-Wujud (Unity of Being) in his monumental Fusus al-Hikam; he taught that all of creation is a theophany (manifestation of God) and that the universe exists so God can know Himself through His creatures.

The ritual calendar of ancient Rome included 40+ official festivals in a year, with the Saturnalia (December 17–23) being the most popular; slaves and masters temporarily exchanged roles, gifts were exchanged, and gambling was permitted — practices whose winter timing and gift-giving traditions scholars have noted parallel the later Christian Christmas celebrations.

Sunni Islam's most authoritative hadith collections, the Kutub al-Sittah (Six Books), include Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim as the most reliable; al-Bukhari reportedly examined 600,000 hadith traditions and accepted only 7,275 as authentic — applying criteria including the moral character of each narrator in the chain of transmission (isnad).

The Aztec Tlaloc, god of rain, agriculture, and water, is one of the oldest deities in Mesoamerica, with evidence of his worship dating back to the Teotihuacan civilization (c. 200 BCE–750 CE); child sacrifices were dedicated to Tlaloc because their tears were believed to stimulate rain, and excavations of the Templo Mayor have revealed chambers full of child remains.

The Protestant work ethic, analyzed by sociologist Max Weber in The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1905), argued that Calvinist predestination created anxiety about election and that disciplined hard work, frugality, and reinvestment of profits were psychological responses; Weber proposed this created the cultural conditions for modern capitalism in northern Europe.

Taoism's Zhuangzi (4th century BCE) is considered one of the world's great philosophical texts and works of literature; it uses absurdist parables, comic anecdotes, and paradoxes — like the story of Zhuangzi dreaming he was a butterfly then waking to wonder if he was a butterfly dreaming of being human — to challenge all fixed categories of thought.

The world's first interfaith dialogue in modern history is often traced to the World's Parliament of Religions held in Chicago in 1893 alongside the World's Columbian Exposition; representatives of Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, Buddhism, Shinto, and other traditions gathered together for the first time, with Swami Vivekananda's speech as the iconic moment.

The Sikh concept of Seva (selfless service) holds that serving humanity is equivalent to serving God; the tradition of Sangat (holy congregation) and Pangat (sitting in a row regardless of caste to eat together) institutionalized equality through shared service, making Sikhism one of the first religious traditions to systematically challenge the caste hierarchy through practice rather than just philosophy.

The medieval Islamic philosopher Abu Hamid al-Ghazali (1058–1111) argued in The Incoherence of the Philosophers (Tahafut al-Falasifa) that Aristotelian philosophy is incompatible with Islamic theology; his critique effectively ended rationalist philosophy's dominance in Sunni Islam, though Ibn Rushd's counter-argument (Incoherence of the Incoherence) preserved the philosophical tradition.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints operates the world's largest genealogical database, FamilySearch, which contains 13+ billion names; begun as a theological project to enable proxy baptisms for the dead, it has become an invaluable resource for secular researchers and is freely accessible to the public worldwide.

The Nicene and Chalcedonian Christology formulas — that Jesus is 'fully divine and fully human' in 'one person with two natures' — were not self-evident from the New Testament but emerged from intense debates over 400+ years; rejected alternatives included Arianism (Jesus is divine but subordinate), Docetism (Jesus only appeared human), and Nestorianism (two persons in Christ).

The Hindu Bhakti movement (6th–17th centuries CE) produced some of India's greatest vernacular literature and music; poet-saints like Kabir, Mirabai, Tukaram, and Andal composed devotional songs in regional languages (Tamil, Marathi, Hindi) accessible to all castes and both sexes, challenging Brahmanical Sanskrit monopoly on religious expression.

The Native American Church, which blends traditional Indigenous spiritual practices with Christian elements and uses the peyote cactus as a sacrament, was founded in the early 20th century; after legal challenges, a 1994 amendment to the American Indian Religious Freedom Act specifically protected Native Americans' right to use peyote in religious ceremonies.

The Sacred Band of Thebes, an elite ancient Greek military unit (378–338 BCE) composed entirely of 150 male couples based on the theory that lovers would fight more bravely alongside each other, was connected to the religious cult of the Sacred Marriage (hieros gamos) between Zeus and Hera, demonstrating how ancient Greek religion and military practice were intertwined.

The Baha'i Faith prohibits clergy, formal rituals, and monastic orders, instead emphasizing personal study of scripture, elected administrative institutions, and the integration of prayer with work and service; the Administrative Order, consisting of Local and National Spiritual Assemblies elected by all adult members, was designed by Baha'u'llah to prevent the consolidation of religious authority.

The Dead Sea Sect of the Qumran community, who produced the Dead Sea Scrolls, believed they were living at the 'end of days' and withdrew into the Judean desert to await the War of the Sons of Light against the Sons of Darkness; their community rule (Serekh ha-Yahad) reveals a strictly hierarchical, celibate (or partly celibate) community practicing ritual baths and communal meals.

Sikhism's Golden Temple complex includes the Akal Takht (Throne of the Timeless One), the highest seat of Sikh religious authority, which faces the Golden Temple across the pool; the Akal Takht was built by the sixth Guru, Hargobind Sahib Ji, and is used to deliberate on matters of Sikh concern and issue religious edicts called hukamnamas.

The Greek philosophical school of Neoplatonism, founded by Plotinus (205–270 CE), taught that reality emanates from the One (God) through successive levels (Nous/Mind, World Soul, Matter); it became the last great pagan intellectual tradition and profoundly influenced Christian (Augustine), Jewish (Maimonides), and Islamic (al-Farabi) theology before the Arab conquest ended its institutional centers.

The Jewish holiday of Sukkot (Feast of Tabernacles/Booths) requires Jews to eat and sleep in temporary outdoor booths (sukkot) for seven days, commemorating the 40 years of desert wandering; its agricultural harvest dimension made it the most joyous of the three pilgrimage festivals, and Zechariah 14:16 envisions all nations eventually coming to Jerusalem to celebrate it.

The Sephardic Jewish tradition, descended from Jews expelled from Spain in 1492 and Portugal in 1497, preserved the medieval Judeo-Spanish language Ladino; these communities settled across the Ottoman Empire (Turkey, Greece, Bulgaria, Israel) and developed a distinct religious culture, liturgical music (piyyutim), and legal traditions different from Ashkenazi (Central/Eastern European) Judaism.

The Islamic institution of Waqf (charitable endowment), in which property is donated in perpetuity for religious or charitable purposes, was one of the most important institutions of Islamic civilization; mosques, hospitals, schools (madrasas), libraries, and caravanserais were funded through waqf, making it the primary mechanism of civil society in the pre-modern Islamic world.

The Theravada Buddhist Vinaya (monastic code) includes a rule that monks may not eat after noon — a practice still observed by Theravada monks in Thailand, Sri Lanka, and Myanmar; this practice, called One Meal Before Noon rule (Eka-bhattika), enables the monk to spend the remainder of the day in meditation without the digestive heaviness associated with evening meals.

The Mandala, derived from the Sanskrit word for circle, serves as a sacred cosmological map in Hindu and Buddhist traditions; the Tibetan Buddhist cosmic mandala (Kalachakra mandala) depicts a five-dimensional divine palace with 722 resident deities and is used as the support for advanced meditations; the Jungian psychologist Carl Jung independently developed mandala drawing as a psychotherapeutic tool.

The Latter-day Saint practice of tithing — donating 10% of one's annual income to the Church — generates an estimated $7 billion per year, making the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints one of the wealthiest religious organizations in the world; in 2020, a whistleblower claimed the Church held $100 billion in investment funds, raising questions about its tax-exempt status.

The Hindu pilgrimage festival of Rath Yatra (Chariot Festival) at the Jagannath Temple in Puri, Odisha, involves massive wooden chariots carrying the deities Jagannath, Balabhadra, and Subhadra through the streets; the English word 'juggernaut' (an unstoppable force) derives from 'Jagannath' after European travelers described pilgrims throwing themselves under the chariot wheels — an exaggerated account now known to be largely mythological.

The concept of Shabbat (Sabbath) in Judaism — ceasing all creative work from Friday sunset to Saturday nightfall — is based on God's rest after the six days of creation (Genesis 2:2–3); traditional halachic interpretation identifies 39 categories of forbidden labor on Shabbat derived from the types of work used to build the Tabernacle in the wilderness, including writing, cooking, and carrying objects in public spaces.

The Igbo Odinani traditional religion of southeastern Nigeria centers on Chi (personal guardian spirit), Chukwu (the supreme deity), and a pantheon of Alusi (lesser deities/forces); Odinani was systematically suppressed by Christian missionaries in the 19th–20th centuries but has experienced revival movements, and its influence persists in Igbo culture and in the diaspora.

The Catholic practice of the Stations of the Cross — a series of 14 images depicting Jesus's journey to crucifixion — became a global devotion from the 15th century after Franciscans popularized it as a spiritual substitute for pilgrimage to Jerusalem; Pope John Paul II added a 15th station (the Resurrection) in 1991, and various communities have adapted the stations to meditate on contemporary suffering.

The Sikh sacred pool (Amrit Sarovar) surrounding the Golden Temple was excavated under the supervision of Guru Ram Das (the fourth Guru) in 1577; its name means 'Pool of the Nectar of Immortality,' and bathing in its waters is considered spiritually purifying — the practice of ritual bathing in sacred waters (istan) has ancient roots in Indic religious traditions.

The philosophy of Religious Pluralism, developed by John Hick in his 1989 book An Interpretation of Religion, argues that all major world religions are culturally conditioned responses to the same ultimate transcendent reality (the Real); while influential in interfaith dialogue, it has been criticized by exclusivists who hold that their own tradition alone is salvifically true.

Hanukkah, the Jewish Festival of Lights, commemorates the rededication of the Temple in Jerusalem in 165 BCE after the Maccabean revolt against Seleucid Greek rule; the central miracle is that a one-day supply of consecrated oil kept the Temple menorah burning for eight days; rabbinically speaking, Hanukkah is a minor holiday that became culturally prominent in the West due to its proximity to Christmas.

The Islamic concept of Taqlid (following the authority of established legal schools without independent reasoning) was debated throughout Islamic history; reformers like Ibn Taymiyya (1263–1328) and later Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703–1792) called for return to direct Quran and hadith study, rejecting taqlid and laying groundwork for Wahhabi/Salafi Islam.

The practice of Buddhist dana (generosity/giving) forms the foundation of lay Buddhist practice; the Pali Canon describes dana as the first of the ten perfections (paramis) because it begins the process of loosening attachment; in Theravada countries, the economic institution of monastic support — laypeople feeding monks daily — structures the entire relationship between Buddhism and society.

The Book of Revelation, the final book of the Christian New Testament, was written during Roman persecution (c. 95 CE) and uses coded symbolic language identifying Rome as 'Babylon' and the emperor Domitian as the Beast; its number 666 (or 616 in some manuscripts) is a gematria code — letters of Nero Caesar in Hebrew numerology — a fact lost for centuries until modern scholarship decoded it.

The spread of Christianity to sub-Saharan Africa predates European colonialism significantly; the Kingdom of Aksum (Ethiopia) converted to Christianity around 330 CE under King Ezana, making it one of the world's first Christian states, and the Kingdom of Kongo converted in 1491 CE before sustained Portuguese contact; Africa now has the world's fastest-growing Christian population.

The Jewish mystical tradition of Kabbalah teaches that the Torah contains hidden divine wisdom encoded at multiple levels; the PaRDeS (orchard) hermeneutic identifies four levels: Peshat (literal), Remez (allegorical), Derash (homiletical), and Sod (mystical/secret) — the acronym PaRDeS forming the Hebrew word for 'paradise,' suggesting that entering deep Torah interpretation is itself a heavenly experience.

The concept of Avatar (digital online persona) derives its name from the Sanskrit/Hindu 'avatara' (divine descent/incarnation); the word was introduced into computing in 1985 by Lucasfilm's Habitat virtual world game, and its current meaning — a digital representation of a person — is a direct metaphorical borrowing from Hindu theology about divine manifestation in human form.

The Daoist immortality quest (xian) aimed at achieving physical immortality through a combination of breathing exercises, dietary restrictions, sexual practices, alchemical elixirs, and meditation; the pursuit of longevity and immortality in religious Taoism produced sophisticated systems of bodily cultivation that influenced Traditional Chinese Medicine, qigong, and tai chi.

The Zoroastrian Avesta, the sacred scripture, was originally transmitted orally for centuries before being written down; only one-quarter to one-third of the original Avesta survives today, the rest having been lost — possibly destroyed during Alexander the Great's conquest of Persia (330 BCE) or subsequent upheavals, making Zoroastrianism one of the great 'incomplete' scripture traditions.

The Christian mystic Julian of Norwich (c. 1343–c. 1416), the first woman to write a book in English (Revelations of Divine Love), described her 16 visions of Christ's passion received during a near-fatal illness; her famous declaration 'All shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well' articulates an optimistic mystical universalism rarely expressed in medieval Christianity.

The Sufi concept of the Qutb (Pole or Axis) holds that at every moment in history there exists one supreme saint through whom divine grace flows to the world; this individual is unknown to most people but sustains cosmic order; the hierarchy of saints below the Qutb includes the abdal (substitutes) and awtad (pillars) who together form an invisible spiritual government of the world.

The Hindu tradition of Utsava Murti (festival deity), a portable bronze image taken out of the temple for processions and public darshan, developed because the main temple icon (mula bera) was permanently enshrined and could not be moved; these festival deities receive a different kind of worship than the fixed icon and are dressed, crowned, and paraded through the streets in elaborate processions.

The concept of Religious Nones — people who identify with no religion — has grown dramatically in the United States, rising from 16% of the population in 2007 to 26% in 2019 according to Pew Research; most Nones are not atheists but rather religiously unaffiliated people who may hold spiritual beliefs and practices outside institutional religion.

The Hindu Brahmacharya ideal of celibacy and student discipline originated as the first of the four life stages; in its modern form, figures like Gandhi incorporated brahmacharya as a spiritual discipline into political activism, believing that sexual abstinence sublimated vital energy (ojas) into spiritual and social power — though modern critics have sharply questioned this philosophy.

Umberto Eco's novel The Name of the Rose (1980), set in a 14th-century Italian monastery, features a poisoned copy of Aristotle's second book of Poetics (on comedy) that a conservative monk kills to prevent laughter from becoming theologically acceptable; the fictional premise reflects a real medieval debate about whether Christ ever laughed, with most early theologians arguing he did not.

The Soto school of Zen Buddhism, brought to Japan by Dogen Zenji (1200–1253) from China, practices shikantaza ('just sitting' meditation) in which there is no object of meditation, no counting of breaths, no koan — just completely open awareness; Dogen's philosophy that 'practice is enlightenment' (shusho ichinyo) is one of Zen Buddhism's most distinctive and profound teachings.

The Ugaritic texts discovered at Ras Shamra, Syria, since 1929 have transformed understanding of ancient Canaanite religion; they reveal a pantheon headed by El and Baal, religious texts with striking parallels to Hebrew biblical imagery, and ritual practices that explain numerous biblical polemics against Baal worship — showing that Israelite monotheism emerged gradually from a polytheistic background.

The Islamic concept of Ilm (knowledge/learning) is so central to the faith that the first word revealed to Muhammad was 'Iqra' (Read/Recite); seeking knowledge is described in hadith as a religious obligation, and the Islamic civilization's libraries — including the House of Wisdom in Baghdad — preserved and extended Greek, Persian, and Indian knowledge during Europe's medieval period.

The Adi Shankara (788–820 CE), one of Hinduism's greatest philosophers, traveled across India on foot debating scholars of all traditions and establishing four mathas (monastic centers) at the four geographic corners of India to organize and revitalize Advaita Vedanta; he is credited with synthesizing Hinduism into a coherent tradition that could withstand Buddhist philosophical challenges.

The Coptic calendar used by Egypt's Coptic Orthodox Church is based on the ancient Egyptian civil calendar and begins on August 29 or 30 of the Gregorian calendar; it preserves ancient Egyptian month names like Thout, Baba, and Hathor, making it one of the oldest continuously used calendrical systems in the world — a living link to pharaonic Egypt.

The Hindu concept of Guru (spiritual teacher, literally 'heavy one' or 'one who dispels darkness') occupies an extraordinary place in Indian spirituality; the Guru-shishya (teacher-disciple) relationship is considered the essential vehicle for spiritual transmission, and some traditions like Kashmir Shaivism hold that liberation (mukti) is impossible without the Guru's direct transmission (shaktipat).

The Islamic Golden Rule, expressed by the Prophet Muhammad in a hadith: 'None of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself,' has exact parallels in virtually every major world religion — Confucius, Hillel, Jesus, and Mahavira all expressed similar formulations, leading some scholars to call it the universal ethical principle of all humanity's religious traditions.

The Mormons' journey westward under Brigham Young (1846–1847) from Nauvoo, Illinois, to the Salt Lake Valley was explicitly modeled on the biblical Exodus; Young cast himself as Moses, the Rocky Mountains as the wilderness, and Utah as the Promised Land — making it one of the clearest examples of typological religious self-understanding in American history.

The Bosnian War (1992–1995) involved deliberate destruction of religious heritage as a weapon of cultural genocide; the National and University Library of Bosnia and Herzegovina, housing 1.5 million volumes and irreplaceable manuscripts, was burned by Serbian nationalist forces in 1992, and over 1,200 mosques were destroyed or damaged — among the greatest losses of Islamic architectural heritage in the 20th century.

The Jain concept of the Tirthankara's Samavasarana (divine assembly hall) describes a perfectly circular assembly where all beings — gods, humans, animals, and supernatural beings — gather to hear the Tirthankara's teaching; the spatial arrangement symbolizes perfect equality among all life forms in the divine presence, a visual statement of Jain universal compassion.

The tradition of the Hajj's Tawaf — circling the Kaaba seven times counterclockwise — is understood by Islamic mystics as mirroring the movement of angels around the divine throne and of electrons around an atomic nucleus; the black stone at the Kaaba's corner is kissed or pointed to at each circuit, linking each pilgrim to the chain of all Muslims who have performed this rite since Abraham.

The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5–7), Jesus's most extended ethical teaching, includes the Beatitudes, the Lord's Prayer, and radical commands such as loving enemies, turning the other cheek, and forgiving without limit; its ethical demands were considered so impractical by many that Martin Luther developed the doctrine of two kingdoms to explain why secular governments cannot be governed by its principles.

The Sikh concept of Waheguru's Hukam (divine will/order) holds that everything in creation operates according to God's will; the Guru Granth Sahib opens with the Mool Mantar and continues with Japji Sahib, in which Guru Nanak concludes that the only way to experience divine union is to accept the Hukam completely — a concept that resolves the tension between free will and divine sovereignty differently than either Calvinist predestination or Islamic qada.

The Aztec creation mythology in the Popol Vuh (a Mayan text with Aztec parallels) describes several failed attempts at creating humans — from mud and wood — before gods finally succeeded with maize; this corn-based anthropogony reflects the agricultural centrality of maize in Mesoamerican civilization and is a founding myth with no parallel in Old World religious traditions.

The Islamic calendar (Hijri) is a purely lunar calendar of 354 or 355 days, making it 10–11 days shorter than the solar year; this means Islamic festivals like Ramadan and Hajj rotate through all seasons of the year over a 33-year cycle, unlike the Jewish lunar-solar calendar which adds a leap month to keep festivals in the same season.

The Marcionite heresy, condemned by the early Church around 144 CE, taught that the God of the Old Testament (a wrathful creator god) was inferior to and distinct from the loving Father of Jesus Christ; Marcion created the first Christian biblical canon, consisting of edited Pauline letters and a truncated Luke's Gospel, which provoked the mainstream Church to develop its own authoritative canon.

The historical Buddha's first teaching at Deer Park near Varanasi, known as the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (Setting the Wheel of Dhamma in Motion), introduced the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path to five former companions; this event is commemorated as Asalha Puja (Dharma Day) in Theravada countries and marks the beginning of the Buddhist monastic community (Sangha).

The Abrahamic tradition's three great monotheisms (Judaism, Christianity, Islam) all trace their spiritual lineage to Abraham (Ibrahim), but describe different aspects of his story as most significant: Jews emphasize his covenant and circumcision, Christians his faith as a model of justification, and Muslims his submission to God's command to sacrifice his son and his rebuilding of the Kaaba.

The Tibetan Book of the Dead's tradition of phowa (transference of consciousness) — in which a trained practitioner guides the dying person's awareness out through the crown of the head at the moment of death toward a higher rebirth or liberation — is one of the world's most elaborate sets of dying practices and has influenced modern Western hospice and death-with-dignity movements.

The Pali term Nibbana (Sanskrit: Nirvana), literally 'blowing out' or 'extinguishing,' describes the cessation of craving, hatred, and delusion that constitutes Buddhist liberation; contrary to popular understanding, the Buddha never described what Nirvana positively is — only what it is not — leading to centuries of philosophical debate about whether it is annihilation, a transcendent state, or the nature of mind itself.

The Council of Jerusalem (c. 48–50 CE), described in Acts 15 and Galatians 2, was the first Christian council; it resolved whether Gentile converts must follow Jewish Law (circumcision, dietary laws) — the council decided they need not, a decision that enabled Christianity to become a universal religion rather than a Jewish sect and set it on its path to global expansion.

Thich Nhat Hanh (1926–2022), the Vietnamese Buddhist monk who developed 'Engaged Buddhism' — applying Buddhist principles to social and political activism — was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize in 1967 by Martin Luther King Jr.; his concept of Interbeing (interexistence of all phenomena) has influenced environmental ethics, psychology, and contemplative practices worldwide.

The Eucharist (Holy Communion) is Christianity's central ritual, commemorating Jesus's Last Supper; denominations disagree profoundly about what happens during it — Catholics hold transubstantiation (bread and wine become Christ's body and blood), Lutherans hold consubstantiation (Christ is present with the elements), Calvinists hold spiritual presence, and most Protestants hold it is a memorial only.

The Namdhari (Kuka) Sikh sect, founded by Baba Balak Singh (1797–1862) and led after him by Baba Ram Singh, rejected the finality of the Sikh Guru lineage and claimed a living human Guru; they were among the first Indians to non-violently resist British colonial rule, with Baba Ram Singh being exiled by the British to Burma in 1872 for organizing boycotts of foreign goods.

The Pyramid Texts of ancient Egypt (c. 2400–2300 BCE), inscribed on the walls of royal burial chambers in Saqqara, are the oldest known religious texts in the world; they contain spells to ensure the pharaoh's safe passage to the afterlife and eventual union with the sun god Ra, and represent an unbroken tradition of hieroglyphic religious composition lasting 3,000 years.

The Hindu goddess Saraswati, deity of knowledge, music, art, speech, and learning, is depicted holding a veena (stringed instrument), a book, a rosary, and a lotus; her festival Vasant Panchami marks the beginning of spring and is the traditional day for children to learn their first letters and for artists to consecrate their tools and instruments.

The Aleinu prayer, recited at the end of every Jewish prayer service, concludes by looking forward to a day when all nations recognize God's sovereignty and the world is repaired (tikkun olam); written perhaps in 3rd-century Babylon, it was once banned in medieval Europe because the Hebrew phrase 'she-lo asanu' (that He did not make us) was (incorrectly) suspected of being anti-Christian.

The Buddhist concept of Avalokiteshvara (Guanyin in Chinese, Kannon in Japanese), the Bodhisattva of infinite compassion, undergoes a remarkable gender transformation as Buddhism spread from India to East Asia: what began as a male deity in Indian Buddhism became predominantly female in Chinese Buddhism, reflecting different cultural ideas about the feminine as the most natural expression of compassion.

Ramakrishna Paramahamsa (1836–1886), the Hindu mystic of Bengal, practiced intensive devotion to the goddess Kali but also followed Islamic Sufi practices and Christian devotion, reportedly experiencing visions of Muhammad and Jesus; his teaching that 'all religions are true' became the foundation of the Ramakrishna Mission founded by his disciple Vivekananda.

The Sioux Ghost Dance movement of 1890, prophesied by the Paiute visionary Wovoka, promised that correct performance of a specific circular dance would bring dead ancestors back, remove white settlers, and restore the buffalo; the US Army's fear of the movement led to the Wounded Knee Massacre of December 29, 1890, in which approximately 250–300 Lakota people were killed.

The Candomblé religion of Brazil, rooted in the Yoruba traditions brought by enslaved West Africans, identifies Catholic saints with Yoruba orishas (Oxala/Jesus, Iemanja/Our Lady of Navigators, Ogun/St. George); this syncretism was often strategic — allowing enslaved people to worship their African deities under the cover of Catholic saints during the slave era.

The Islamic philosophy of Ibn Sina (Avicenna, 980–1037 CE), whose medical encyclopedia Canon of Medicine remained a standard European medical text until the 17th century, developed a 'floating man' thought experiment — anticipating Descartes' cogito — to argue that the soul knows itself independent of the body; his synthesis of Aristotle with Islamic theology influenced both Islamic and Christian scholasticism.

The Meiji Restoration (1868) in Japan led the new government to artificially separate Shinto from Buddhism, which had been intertwined for over 1,000 years, and to promote State Shinto as a civil religion that deified the Emperor; this State Shinto was formally dismantled by the US occupation after World War II, separating the Emperor from divine status in the 1947 constitution.

The Christian tradition of iconoclasm — destruction of religious images — erupted violently in the Byzantine Empire during the 8th–9th centuries (the Iconoclast Controversy), dividing the empire on whether using images in worship was idolatry; the Second Council of Nicaea (787 CE) settled the matter by distinguishing latria (worship, for God alone) from proskynesis (veneration, acceptable for images).

The Baul tradition of Bengal, India — wandering minstrel-mystics who sing devotional songs rejecting caste, clergy, and formal religion — influenced Rabindranath Tagore and continues today; Bauls search for the 'Man of the Heart' (Maner Manush), a divine being residing within the human body, and their ecstatic songs were inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2008.

The Hindu festival of Onam, celebrated in Kerala for ten days in August-September, commemorates the mythical reign of the demon king Mahabali, whose just and golden rule is remembered with such fondness that the gods arranged for him to return to visit his people once a year; the festival transcends religious boundaries, being celebrated by Hindus, Christians, and Muslims in Kerala alike.

The Lailat al-Qadr (Night of Power or Night of Decree), falling in the last ten days of Ramadan, is described in the Quran as 'better than a thousand months' (97:3); Muslims believe the entire Quran was sent down to the first heaven on this night and that prayers on it are uniquely efficacious; many Muslims spend the entire night in prayer, seeking it on the odd nights of the last ten days of Ramadan.
